title: Harmony and Voice Leading IV: Secondary Function

guide.summary: Unit 7 covers secondary (applied) dominants and leading-tone chords, tonicization, and modulation to closely related keys.

sections.heading: Secondary dominants
sections.body: A secondary dominant is the V or V7 of a chord other than tonic, temporarily treating that chord as a tonic (tonicization). It is labeled V/x or V7/x. In C major: V/V = D F♯ A, V7/V = D F♯ A C, V/ii = A C♯ E, V/vi = E G♯ B, V7/IV = C E G B♭. The chromatic note usually acts as a temporary leading tone resolving up to the root of the target (F♯ → G in V/V → V), and a chordal seventh resolves down. Diminished triads (vii° in major, ii° in minor) cannot be tonicized because they aren't stable chords.

sections.heading: Secondary leading-tone chords
sections.body: vii°/x, vii°7/x, and viiø7/x are leading-tone chords built a half step below the target root. In C major, vii°7/V = F♯ A C E♭, resolving to G. Like secondary dominants, they intensify motion to the target chord.

sections.heading: Modulation
sections.body: Tonicization is brief; modulation establishes a new key, usually confirmed by a cadence. Closely related keys differ from the home key by at most one accidental: for C major, G major, F major, A minor, E minor, and D minor. A common pivot-chord modulation uses a chord diatonic to both keys (e.g., A minor = vi in C = ii in G), followed by the new key's dominant and a cadence. Direct (phrase) modulation shifts keys without a pivot, often at a phrase boundary.

keyTakeaways: V/x and V7/x tonicize non-tonic chords.
vii°7/x: a half step below the target.
Pivot chords are diatonic in both keys.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the chromatic alteration (F♯ in V/V).
examTips: Spot accidentals to find secondary chords.
Look for a cadence to confirm modulation.

practice.prompt: In C major, realize I – V/V – V – I in four voices (all root position). Use the soprano line E4 – D4 – D4 – E4. Give each voice's pitch and resolve all tendency tones.

rubric.description: I: S E4, A C4, T G3, B C3.
V/V: D F♯ A, e.g., S D4, A A3, T F♯3, B D3 (F♯ not doubled).
V: e.g., S D4, A B3, T G3, B G2.
I: e.g., S E4, A C4, T G3, B C3.
No parallel fifths/octaves (e.g., avoid moving C–G to D–A in parallel).
Identifies the V–I as an IAC (soprano on 3).

practice.sampleResponse:
Chord 1 (I): S E4, A C4, T G3, B C3.
Chord 2 (V/V): S D4, A A3, T F♯3, B D3.
Chord 3 (V): S D4, A B3, T G3, B G2.
Chord 4 (I): S E4, A C4, T G3, B C3.
The tenor's F♯ (the temporary leading tone of G) resolves up to G, and the alto's B resolves up to C in the final chord. Moving the tenor from G down to F♯ while the bass rises avoids the parallel fifths that would occur if bass and tenor moved C–G to D–A. Because the soprano ends on E, the V–I cadence is an imperfect authentic cadence.
